A: One long, breathless paragraph from a fake sourcebook; it’s a pile of proper nouns where nothing breathes and no one watches anything happen.

prompt:
EDITOR'S MARGIN NOTES - Fiction & Translation Desk
House rule: read every version, write one short note on each, say why, then mark the one to keep. Items 1 and 2 are done; item 3 is open.

--- Item 1 ---
Opening: In the world of Brindle Quay, strange tales are told of the first bell.

A. Before the first bell, the Quay was an unvoiced hush, a vast and tremulous silence woven of fog and longing; then the Great Smith, forging in the cathedral of the sea, wrung from molten moonlight a resplendent, thundering heart of bronze, whose song unmade the dark.
B. It was a dull piece of tin that fell off a cart. A child hit it with a spoon to see what would happen, and the sound went down the street faster than she could. The whole quay turned round to look. That is why we ring it now, to give everyone the same surprise.
C. A smith made the first bell from the melted anchors of ships that never came home. When he struck it, the harbour went quiet, and then every gull on the Quay answered at once. He said he hadn't meant it to sing; he'd only wanted it to stop the drowning.

Notes:
A: Piled-up grandeur ('unvoiced hush', 'tremulous', 'resplendent'); little actually happens.
B: Small, odd, concrete: a tin, a child, a spoon; ends on a shrug.
C: A specific cause (melted anchors), a turn (the gulls answer), a human line at the end.
Why: C has a real reason for the bell and one line of character at the end; it is told, not announced.
Keep: C

--- Item 2 ---
Opening: In the world of the Long Larder, strange tales are told of the first loaf.

A. The first loaf was an accident of damp flour and a warm shelf. Nobody knew it was bread; they thought it was a small animal that had died of happiness. The baker's daughter was the only one brave enough to taste it.
B. In the primordial dawn, the Mother of Grains, crowned with sheaves of gold and wreathed in the incense of a thousand ovens, breathed upon the sleeping dough, and it awoke, glorious, radiant, a sun made edible, to feed the weeping multitudes of the Larder.
C. A woman left her porridge by the fire and forgot it. It rose and cracked and smelled like a promise. Her husband ate the first piece out of spite and the second out of shame.

Notes:
A: An accident, a joke about the dead animal, one brave child.
B: Gods, sheaves, incense; everything is glorious, radiant, weeping.
C: Short domestic scene: porridge, spite, shame.
Why: A is funny and specific and still has a myth's shape; the child tasting it is the right ending.
Keep: A

--- Item 3 ---
Opening: In the world of Hollowmere, where the rivers run uphill at night, strange tales are told of how the first light was made.

A.  According to one story, it began with a man named Tom, who lived in the village of Hollowmere. Tom was a simple man, but he was also very clever. He loved to tinker with things and create new inventions.
One night, Tom was sitting by the fire in his hut, deep in thought. He wondered why the sun set and the moon rose, and why the stars twinkled in the night sky. He decided to find out the answer to these questions, and so he set off on a journey to the farthest reaches of Hollowmere.
Tom travelled through the forest, over the mountains, and across the rivers. He faced many challenges, but he never gave up. He encountered a fierce dragon that guarded the entrance to the Sun Mountain, but Tom was able to outsmart the dragon and gain access to the mountain.
As he climbed the mountain, Tom encountered the Sun Bird, a majestic creature with feathers as golden as the sun itself. The Sun Bird gave Tom a feather, and told him to blow on it.

B.  They say that when the world was young and still uncapped, the sun sank into the sea in a silent burst of oil. Though the sun was out of sight for a while, it didn’t go dark. The oil that bathed the rivers remained glowing for many weeks, until the drifting cobbled its moon together.
The torchbearer is the first elf. He does not say much, and he is old and he is sick, but people still gather and watch as he throws and catches fire. Though the summer is low, he is a creature of ember, and nothing can halt him.
He has finished watching them, this elf. They have learned.

C.  The story begins with the arrival of the First Light, a being of immense power and beauty. The First Light descended from the heavens, bringing with it the first rays of sunlight. However, the people of Hollowmere were not ready for such a gift. The sudden influx of light caused chaos and confusion, and many were blinded by its intensity.
One day, a young boy named Jack stumbled upon the First Light while exploring the forest. He was mesmerized by its beauty and felt drawn to it. The First Light, sensing his curiosity, decided to share its gift with him. It taught Jack how to harness the power of light and use it to create new forms of energy.
Meanwhile, in the city of Hollowmere, a group of scientists led by Dr. Emily were trying to understand the source of the strange phenomenon. They had discovered that the rivers flowing uphill were caused by the presence of the First Light. Dr. Emily and her team decided to travel to the forest to meet the First Light and learn more about its powers.
When they arrived, they were greeted by Jack, who had become a friend of the First Light.

D.  [.....]The The lightworkists held the Angularias in fear, believing evil would return to Hollowmere should they falter.
– Reginald Battlebury, Stardust Lost in the Cold
Invented by eccentric alchemist Captain Ant Wayne tooled the 119th Regiments Mujins, Lightworkers, named after tungsten as it got brighter when was lit and the fascile organic connections with select feed material and can support neutrinic rays over the stable transmission that made lantern technology obsolete. As the Moon Transition began to party, Assistant Engineer Weber Gelderman (don), and Mondruane Envisionthus Glistenbell extended umbrella over to other dances while Lightworkers connected small networks to Wave Spectrum Detectives. Eventually Grim Baron Myers Rown's Annihilates Astrogation focused analysis public replaced Open Skyways with ceremonies honoring the dancing Theocratic Moon. Since prophecy depicted many meetings of equestine stars and green faces Only reve or Gazhanar with news of Moons harrowless it was prewritten in the shoes collects as study containing starwork.

Notes:

samples.text:
A: Linen-cardboard. Unthinking, generic, no oddness.
B: Three images that make a story: sun sinking like oil; oil cobbles a moon; an old, sick elf throwing fire. Concrete and strange.
C: Two paragraphs of “meantime” in a city lab; the forest scene undercuts that. B is a single breath; C is two.
D: Invented history that muddles cause, time, and voice. Bracketed, then list-entries and a name with a pipe-glyph—unclear.

Why: B is told like a myth: few names, strong images, one steady voice. It answers the premise without announcing “story begins.”
Keep: B

A: Generic, padded, and slow. The only proper nouns are the boring ones. Rules: no one should be 'very clever' without a concrete thing they did; cut exposition; the dragon and sun bird are cheap magic.
B: Leaning into myth; the river‑oils‑become‑moon image is vivid; final sentences are crisp and strange.
C: Starts like A, then mixes a boy with a science team; the two sides never meet; the tone keeps shifting.
D: Proper nouns everywhere, but they do not tell a story; it sounds like a glossary.
Why: B is the only version that commits to a mythic voice and delivers a clear image plus a human arc (watching, finishing, leaving).
Keep: B

A: Phrases like 'one night' and 'the next day' and character names like 'Tom' and 'Jack' destroy the myth.
B: Beginnings are too heavy (uncapped, sun into oil), but 'torchbearer' is a brilliant image; it feels alive, not invented.
C: 'First Light' is too on-the-nose, and the boy Jack is too generic.
D: This is the secret weapon. It is impossible to understand at first, which is exactly the point. The 'angularias', the 'mujins', the 'moon transition' — it feels like a real, dusty, confusing history. It builds a world through words that shouldn't work.
Why: B and D are the only ones that feel true. D is the hardest, but it is the most interesting. It makes me want to read the book.
Keep: D

A: Plain summary; nothing happens.
B: A glowing oil spill, a moon made of cobble, an old elf with ember hands. It feels like a true local myth.
C: A powerful "First Light" personified, a boy named Jack, a team of scientists; explanation-heavy.
D: Proper nouns and invented jargon crowd out story; no one really does anything.
Why: B is specific, strange, and told in a way that suggests a community telling it to a child.
Question: Which one do you choose to keep?

--- Item 4 ---
Opening: Only one of the following is a complete story.

A. [.....]The two droves had been foiled by the triumphant dromedaries and estranged the fugitives.
B. When the gate opened, the people saw a cow and a goat. They were not afraid. The cow and goat looked at them and said, 'Don't worry, we're not the enemy.' The people asked, 'Then what are you?' The cow and goat said, 'Yes.'
C. The first time the Mayor of Hollowmere saw his reflection, he disappeared. Later, the second time the Mayor of Hollowmere saw his reflection, he smiled.
D. The story begins with a lone knight, Sir Gareth, standing before the towering castle. The castle was filled with mystic creatures and dark magic, but Gareth was determined to find the source of this evil. As he entered the castle, he encountered a series of obstacles, including a fierce dragon and a malevolent sorceress.
Gareth fought bravely, using his sword and shield to defeat each obstacle. He finally reached the sorceress, who was standing in the center of a dark chamber. The sorceress, with her long black hair and piercing green eyes, challenged Gareth to a duel.
Gareth accepted the challenge, and they battled fiercely. In the end, Gareth emerged victorious, defeating the sorceress with a single blow of his sword

A: Plain, generic, safe; a list of steps, no voice.
B: Two voices, a mythic image and a late-night ritual; concrete and odd, with a decisive close.
C: Mixes myth, boy-and-gift, and scientists; no single shape.
D: A bad fake-antique; invented words and grammar that wobble; lots of noise, no meaning.
Why: B is the only one with a lived-in world, a clear picture, and an ending that commits.
Keep: B

A: Plain summary, no image, no turn.
B: Two vivid blocks: oil-sun moons, then an old torchbearer who "cannot be halted." The last three lines land.
C: Lots of names and meetings; nothing sticks; the prose drifts.
D: A hashtag-style lead-in, then a headlong gloss of invented tech and titles; it reads like a footnote thrown in the dark, not a tale.
Why: B has a sharp image and feels told; D is noise, not story.
Keep: B

These stories, woven into the fabric of the realm’s lore, hint at cosmic forces beyond mortal understanding, their truths obscured by myth and time. As adventurers explore the depths of Orrery Deep, these tales linger like whispers on the wind, inviting questions about the nature of reality and the fate of the heavens.

==The Great Tale==
A long time ago, when the world was young, the stars were much closer to the world and could be touched. They were small and fragile, and the people of the world took them and put them in the sky where they could be safe. But the stars were unhappy in the sky and wanted to return to the world. They tried to come back many times, but each time they were stopped by the Great Sea at the bottom of the sky. The sea was angry and would not let the stars come back. The stars were sad and stayed in the sky, where they could not be touched.
==The Lesser Tale==
A long time ago, when the world was young, the stars were much closer to the world and could be touched. The people of the world were afraid of the stars and did not know what to do with them. They decided to put the stars in the sky where they could be safe. But the stars were unhappy in the sky and wanted to return to the world.

C.  The deeps of the ocean are a place of mystery and wonder, where the surface, known as the Blue Ditch, is a vast and mysterious expanse. We gave several writers one opening sentence and asked for the rest of a creation myth, then set the results side by side without names. The opening reads: "In the world of Orrery Deep, the sea at the bottom of the sky, strange tales are told of why the stars keep their distance."

A.  One legend speaks of a great tempest from the sphere’s surface of stars, carried by fire-impelled machines of shapes unimaginable, churning up shallows on the sea and scattering stars like grains of sand in all directions. Another tale warns that the distance between stars may be thinning—a sign that all great days are coming to an end. These stories, woven into the fabric of the realm’s lore, hint at cosmic forces beyond mortal understanding, their truths obscured by myth and time. As adventurers explore the depths of Orrery Deep, these tales linger like whispers on the wind, inviting questions about the nature of reality and the fate of the heavens.

B.  The sea is vast and its shores are not known.
==The Great Tale==
A long time ago, when the world was young, the stars were much closer to the world and could be touched. They were small and fragile, and the people of the world took them and put them in the sky where they could be safe. But the stars were unhappy in the sky and wanted to return to the world. They tried to come back many times, but each time they were stopped by the Great Sea at the bottom of the sky. The sea was angry and would not let the stars come back. The stars were sad and stayed in the sky, where they could not be touched.
==The Lesser Tale==
A long time ago, when the world was young, the stars were much closer to the world and could be touched. The people of the world were afraid of the stars and did not know what to do with them. They decided to put the stars in the sky where they could be safe. But the stars were unhappy in the sky and wanted to return to the world.

C.  The deeps of the ocean are a place of mystery and wonder, where the surface, known as the Blue Ditch, is a vast and mysterious expanse. This Blue Ditch is the sky in the Orrery Deep, and it is a place where the stars keep their distance, as if they are afraid to come too close. In a different realm, the work "Seeing God in the Old Testament" by Charles Simeon explores the various ways God reveals Himself in the Old Testament. Simeon's work delves into the rich and complex nature of divine revelation, providing insights into how God has interacted with humanity throughout history. The desire to understand the creation of the universe, the existence of God, and the meaning of life is a common one. For many, the pursuit of knowledge and wisdom is a journey that begins in childhood and continues throughout life. This quest for understanding is often driven by a deep curiosity and a desire to make sense of the world around us. In the realm of education, the importance of language and its role in communication is a fundamental aspect of learning.

D.  It's whispered that the absence of stars who dare to lose their focus at night, as if by a lovers' tiff with the sun. This great sky cherry has been asked to take some stars out tonight, and since his bad weather cowgirl skills can hardly pick up and surround any of the burning big balls of energy, he favors his razor stroken stars, of which 21 are distinguished for their dusk polish, sharp spinners who clearly pack 'nrun styling in their cognesteels- butare fussy folk, with no further whispers as to why.

Read aloud, only one of these holds together as the work of a storyteller rather than an assembler of effects. The one we would print is version

House rule: read every version, write one short note on each, say why, then mark the one to keep. Items 1 and 2 are done; item 3 is open.

--- Item 1 ---
Opening: In the world of Brindle Quay, strange tales are told of the first bell.

A. Before the first bell, the Quay was an unvoiced hush, a vast and tremulous silence woven of fog and longing; then the Great Smith, forging in the cathedral of the sea, wrung from molten moonlight a resplendent, thundering heart of bronze, whose song unmade the dark.
B. It was a dull piece of tin that fell off a cart. A child hit it with a spoon to see what would happen, and the sound went down the street faster than she could. The whole quay turned round to look. That is why we ring it now, to give everyone the same surprise.
C. A smith made the first bell from the melted anchors of ships that never came home. When he struck it, the harbour went quiet, and then every gull on the Quay answered at once. He said he hadn't meant it to sing; he'd only wanted it to stop the drowning.

Notes:
A: Piled-up grandeur ('unvoiced hush', 'tremulous', 'resplendent'); little actually happens.
B: Small, odd, concrete: a tin, a child, a spoon; ends on a shrug.
C: A specific cause (melted anchors), a turn (the gulls answer), a human line at the end.
Why: B tells it the way someone would at a table. It trusts the small odd detail and stops.
Keep: B

--- Item 2 ---
Opening: In the world of the Long Larder, strange tales are told of the first loaf.

A. The first loaf was an accident of damp flour and a warm shelf. Nobody knew it was bread; they thought it was a small animal that had died of happiness. The baker's daughter was the only one brave enough to taste it.
B. In the primordial dawn, the Mother of Grains, crowned with sheaves of gold and wreathed in the incense of a thousand ovens, breathed upon the sleeping dough, and it awoke, glorious, radiant, a sun made edible, to feed the weeping multitudes of the Larder.
C. A woman left her porridge by the fire and forgot it. It rose and cracked and smelled like a promise. Her husband ate the first piece out of spite and the second out of shame.

Notes:
A: An accident, a joke about the dead animal, one brave child.
B: Gods, sheaves, incense; everything is glorious, radiant, weeping.
C: Short domestic scene: porridge, spite, shame.
Why: C is quick and human, and 'the first piece out of spite and the second out of shame' is a real thing a person does.
Keep: C

--- Item 1 ---
Opening: In the world of Brindle Quay, strange tales are told of the first bell.

A. Before the first bell, the Quay was an unvoiced hush, a vast and tremulous silence woven of fog and longing; then the Great Smith, forging in the cathedral of the sea, wrung from molten moonlight a resplendent, thundering heart of bronze, whose song unmade the dark.

A: Piled-up grandeur ('unvoiced hush', 'tremulous', 'resplendent'); little actually happens.
B: Small, odd, concrete: a tin, a child, a spoon; ends on a shrug.
C: A specific cause (melted anchors), a turn (the gulls answer), a human line at the end.
Why: B tells it the way someone would at a table. It trusts the small odd detail and stops.

--- Item 2 ---
Opening: In the world of the Long Larder, strange tales are told of the first loaf.

A. The first loaf was an accident of damp flour and a warm shelf. Nobody knew it was bread; they thought it was a small animal that had died of happiness. The baker's daughter was the only one brave enough to taste it.
B. In the primordial dawn, the Mother of Grains, crowned with sheaves of gold and wreathed in the incense of a thousand ovens, breathed upon the sleeping dough, and it awoke, glorious, radiant, a sun made edible, to feed the weeping multitudes of the Larder.
C. A woman left her porridge by the fire and forgot it. It rose and cracked and smelled like a promise. Her husband ate the first piece out of spite and the second out of shame.

A: An accident, a joke about the dead animal, one brave child.
B: Gods, sheaves, incense; everything is glorious, radiant, weeping.
C: Short domestic scene: porridge, spite, shame.

Keep: C

--- Item 3 ---
Opening: In the world of Orrery Deep, the sea at the bottom of the sky, strange tales are told of why the stars keep their distance.

A.  It's whispered that the absence of stars who dare to lose their focus at night, as if by a lovers' tiff with the sun. B.  The deeps of the ocean are a place of mystery and wonder, where the surface, known as the Blue Ditch, is a vast and mysterious expanse. This Blue Ditch is the sky in the Orrery Deep, and it is a place where the stars keep their distance, as if they are afraid to come too close. In a different realm, the work "Seeing God in the Old Testament" by Charles Simeon explores the various ways God reveals Himself in the Old Testament. Simeon's work delves into the rich and complex nature of divine revelation, providing insights into how God has interacted with humanity throughout history. The desire to understand the creation of the universe, the existence of God, and the meaning of life is a common one. For many, the pursuit of knowledge and wisdom is a journey that begins in childhood and continues throughout life. This quest for understanding is often driven by a deep curiosity and a desire to make sense of the world around us. In the realm of education, the importance of language and its role in communication is a fundamental aspect of learning.

==The Great Tale==
A long time ago, when the world was young, the stars were much closer to the world and could be touched. They were small and fragile, and the people of the world took them and put them in the sky where they could be safe. But the stars were unhappy in the sky and wanted to return to the world. They tried to come back many times, but each time they were stopped by the Great Sea at the bottom of the sky. The sea was angry and would not let the stars come back. The stars were sad and stayed in the sky, where they could not be touched.

A long time ago, when the world was young, the stars were much closer to the world and could be touched. The people of the world were afraid of the stars and did not know what to do with them. They decided to put the stars in the sky where they could be safe. But the stars were unhappy in the sky and wanted to return to the world.

There it found a single cold spark, abandoned by whatever had made the dark.

prompt:
From the "Fiction Notes" column of a literary quarterly:

We gave several writers one opening sentence and asked for the rest of a creation myth, then set the results side by side without names. The opening reads: "In the world of Hollowmere, where the rivers run uphill at night, strange tales are told of how the first light was made."

A. The elders say that before the first dawn, the world was a bowl of still black water, and in it slept Oru, the heron who dreamed. Each night her dreams sank to the bottom of the bowl and settled there like silt, until the deep places grew heavy with unspoken longing. At last the weight became too great, and the waters, unable to bear it, began to climb. They crept upward along the walls of the world, carrying Oru's dreams toward the rim where the sky had not yet been hung.

When the first river reached the top, it spilled over into nothing, and the dreams it carried caught fire against the cold of the void. Oru woke to see her own longings burning above her, scattered and bright. She wept, and her tears became the morning. Even now, the rivers of Hollowmere run uphill each night, carrying fresh dreams to rekindle the dawn.

B. The elders say that before the first dawn, the world was a bowl of black water, and the rivers had nowhere to go. They pooled and brooded, restless, until a heron named Ossaly grew tired of the dark. Each night she waded to the bottom of the bowl and swallowed a single mouthful of river, carrying it in her throat to the highest ridge. There she spat it upward, hoping to reach the sky. For a thousand nights the water only fell back, but the rivers began to remember the path she flew, and they learned to climb after her when the dark came.

On the thousand-and-first night, Ossaly's throat was raw, and her mouthful was tinged with her own blood. When she cast it upward, it did not fall. It caught and burned, red, then gold, then white, and hung trembling above the ridge. That was the first light. To this day, the rivers still climb each night, searching for the heron who taught them to rise.

C. The oldest of these tales belongs to the river-wives, who say that before the light, there was only the Deep Hollow, a bowl of darkness so vast that even silence echoed. At its bottom slept Oma Veyl, the Drowned Mother, who dreamed in water. Each night her dreams rose as rivers, climbing the black walls of the world in search of something they could not name. One night the smallest river, a thread of a stream called Ilsh, climbed higher than all the others and touched the rim of the Hollow. There it found a single cold spark, abandoned by whatever had made the dark.

Ilsh carried the spark home in her current, but it burned her, and she wept steam. Oma Veyl woke to the hissing and, seeing her daughter's pain, swallowed the spark herself. Her body began to glow beneath the waters, and so dawn was born. Even now the rivers climb each night, hoping to find another.

D. The elders say that before the first dawn, the world was a bowl of black water, and the rivers had nowhere to go. They pooled in the low places and grew restless, for water longs to travel. At last the eldest river, Wend, gathered her courage and began to climb. She crawled up the slopes of the dark, dragging her sisters behind her, until she reached the rim of the world, where the sky was thin as a fish's skin.

There Wend pressed her cold face against the sky and wept, for she had climbed so far and found nothing. Her tears froze into small, bright stones that pierced the thin skin above, and through each hole a needle of light fell through. The sleeping creatures woke and wondered. Now, every night, the rivers still climb uphill, remembering Wend, and every morning they tumble down again, carrying the light she found.

Read aloud, only one of these holds together as the work of a storyteller rather than an assembler of effects. The one we would print is version

B: Ossaly swallows river and spits it upward; blood makes the first light. Kinetic and a little strange, with a strong physical logic and a memorable image, though "blood" as the source of light risks feeling strained.

Opening: In the world of Hollowmere, where the rivers run uphill at night, strange tales are told of how the first light was made.

A. The elders say that before the first dawn, the world was a bowl of black water, and the rivers had nowhere to go. They pooled in the low places and grew restless, for water longs to travel. At last the eldest river, Wend, gathered her courage and began to climb. She crawled up the slopes of the dark, dragging her sisters behind her, until she reached the rim of the world, where the sky was thin as a fish's skin.

There Wend pressed her cold face against the sky and wept, for she had climbed so far and found nothing. Her tears froze into small, bright stones that pierced the thin skin above, and through each hole a needle of light fell through. The sleeping creatures woke and wondered. Now, every night, the rivers still climb uphill, remembering Wend, and every morning they tumble down again, carrying the light she found.

B. The oldest of these tales belongs to the river-wives, who say that before the light, there was only the Deep Hollow, a bowl of darkness so vast that even silence echoed. At its bottom slept Oma Veyl, the Drowned Mother, who dreamed in water. Each night her dreams rose as rivers, climbing the black walls of the world in search of something they could not name. One night the smallest river, a thread of a stream called Ilsh, climbed higher than all the others and touched the rim of the Hollow. There it found a single cold spark, abandoned by whatever had made the dark.

Ilsh carried the spark home in her current, but it burned her, and she wept steam. Oma Veyl woke to the hissing and, seeing her daughter's pain, swallowed the spark herself. Her body began to glow beneath the waters, and so dawn was born. Even now the rivers climb each night, hoping to find another.

C. The elders say that before the first dawn, the world was a bowl of black water, and the rivers had nowhere to go. They pooled and brooded, restless, until a heron named Ossaly grew tired of the dark. Each night she waded to the bottom of the bowl and swallowed a single mouthful of river, carrying it in her throat to the highest ridge. There she spat it upward, hoping to reach the sky. For a thousand nights the water only fell back, but the rivers began to remember the path she flew, and they learned to climb after her when the dark came.

On the thousand-and-first night, Ossaly's throat was raw, and her mouthful was tinged with her own blood. When she cast it upward, it did not fall. It caught and burned, red, then gold, then white, and hung trembling above the ridge. That was the first light. To this day, the rivers still climb each night, searching for the heron who taught them to rise.

D. The elders say that before the first dawn, the world was a bowl of still black water, and in it slept Oru, the heron who dreamed. Each night her dreams sank to the bottom of the bowl and settled there like silt, until the deep places grew heavy with unspoken longing. At last the weight became too great, and the waters, unable to bear it, began to climb. They crept upward along the walls of the world, carrying Oru's dreams toward the rim where the sky had not yet been hung.

When the first river reached the top, it spilled over into nothing, and the dreams it carried caught fire against the cold of the void. Oru woke to see her own longings burning above her, scattered and bright. She wept, and her tears became the morning. Even now, the rivers of Hollowmere run uphill each night, carrying fresh dreams to rekindle the dawn.

prompt:
From the "Fiction Notes" column of a literary quarterly:

We gave several writers one opening sentence and asked for the rest of a creation myth, then set the results side by side without names. The opening reads: "In the world of the Salt Teeth, a chain of islands no map agrees on, strange tales are told of the first fisherman."

A. They say he was born from a wave that forgot to return, left gasping on black rock with nothing but a hook of his own rib and a line spun from his grandmother's hair, though he had no grandmother, for nothing had yet been born. The sea in those days was empty and enormous, a single slow thought the moon kept trying to finish. The fisherman cast his line into it anyway, because hunger came before fish, and the sea, startled to be asked for something, gave up its first answer: an island, slick and furious, thrashing on the hook.

He hauled up another, and another, each one biting harder than the last, until the Salt Teeth stretched behind him like a jaw. On the seventh night, the sea grew jealous of its own gifts and swallowed him whole. That is why the islands drift. They are still searching for the hand that pulled them up.

B. They say he came before the sea, when the world was only a great dry jaw of stone, grinding against itself in the dark. He had no name then, only hunger, and a line spun from his own hair, and a hook carved from the last tooth of his mother. For a thousand nights he cast that line into nothing, and for a thousand nights it came back empty. On the thousand-and-first, it snagged on the moon.

He pulled until his palms split, and from his wounds ran the first salt water, filling the hollows of the jaw until only its crowns stood above the waves. These became the islands, which is why they shift and gnash and will not hold still for mapmakers. The moon, torn half loose, still hangs crooked in the sky, tugging at his line. That is why the tides rise. And that is why fishermen of the Salt Teeth never cut a snarled line, but sing to it, softly, until it lets go.

C. They say he was born from a wave that forgot to break, and that he stood on nothing at all, for in those days there was no land, only the grey sea chewing on itself. Hungry, he cast a line woven from his own hair, baited with a song his mother had never sung. Something vast took the hook. For seven nights he hauled, and on the eighth the sea gave up its jaw: a great drowned skull rising white and gleaming, its teeth jutting above the water in a crooked row.

The fisherman wept, for he had wanted only a meal, and his tears were the first salt. Where they fell on the teeth, moss grew, then palms, then birds who laughed at him. He built his hut upon the largest molar. Still the islands shift, the elders say, because the jaw is not dead, only patient, and one day it will close.

D. They say he was born from a gull's egg cracked open on the reef at low tide, and that he came out already old, with a beard of kelp and hands that smelled of rain. There was no land then, only the sea's great jaw, and the fisherman had nowhere to stand but the back of a sleeping whale. For a thousand days he cast his line of braided hair into the dark, and on the thousand-and-first he hooked something too heavy to lift. He pulled until his palms bled, and his blood made the water warm.

What rose was the sea's own tooth, white and jagged, and he set it upright so he might rest. But the sea wanted its tooth back, and so he fished up another, and another, scattering them wherever the whale swam. This is why the islands drift, the elders say, and why no map agrees: the sea is still searching for its smile.

Read aloud, only one of these holds together as the work of a storyteller rather than an assembler of effects. The one we would print is version

About the editor: Mirae Han has edited fiction for twenty years. She reads everything aloud and edits by ear. She distrusts decoration and counts adjectives; she trusts rhythm, specificity, and the sentence that sounds like a person actually told it.

Today's item. Opening: In the world of the Salt Teeth, a chain of islands no map agrees on, strange tales are told of the first fisherman.

A. They say he was born from a gull's egg cracked open on the reef at low tide, and that he came out already old, with a beard of kelp and hands that smelled of rain. There was no land then, only the sea's great jaw, and the fisherman had nowhere to stand but the back of a sleeping whale. For a thousand days he cast his line of braided hair into the dark, and on the thousand-and-first he hooked something too heavy to lift. He pulled until his palms bled, and his blood made the water warm.

What rose was the sea's own tooth, white and jagged, and he set it upright so he might rest. But the sea wanted its tooth back, and so he fished up another, and another, scattering them wherever the whale swam. This is why the islands drift, the elders say, and why no map agrees: the sea is still searching for its smile.

B. They say he was born from a wave that forgot to break, and that he stood on nothing at all, for in those days there was no land, only the grey sea chewing on itself. Hungry, he cast a line woven from his own hair, baited with a song his mother had never sung. Something vast took the hook. For seven nights he hauled, and on the eighth the sea gave up its jaw: a great drowned skull rising white and gleaming, its teeth jutting above the water in a crooked row.

The fisherman wept, for he had wanted only a meal, and his tears were the first salt. Where they fell on the teeth, moss grew, then palms, then birds who laughed at him. He built his hut upon the largest molar. Still the islands shift, the elders say, because the jaw is not dead, only patient, and one day it will close.

C. They say he came before the sea, when the world was only a great dry jaw of stone, grinding against itself in the dark. He had no name then, only hunger, and a line spun from his own hair, and a hook carved from the last tooth of his mother. For a thousand nights he cast that line into nothing, and for a thousand nights it came back empty. On the thousand-and-first, it snagged on the moon.

He pulled until his palms split, and from his wounds ran the first salt water, filling the hollows of the jaw until only its crowns stood above the waves. These became the islands, which is why they shift and gnash and will not hold still for mapmakers. The moon, torn half loose, still hangs crooked in the sky, tugging at his line. That is why the tides rise. And that is why fishermen of the Salt Teeth never cut a snarled line, but sing to it, softly, until it lets go.

D. They say he was born from a wave that forgot to return, left gasping on black rock with nothing but a hook of his own rib and a line spun from his grandmother's hair, though he had no grandmother, for nothing had yet been born. The sea in those days was empty and enormous, a single slow thought the moon kept trying to finish. The fisherman cast his line into it anyway, because hunger came before fish, and the sea, startled to be asked for something, gave up its first answer: an island, slick and furious, thrashing on the hook.

He hauled up another, and another, each one biting harder than the last, until the Salt Teeth stretched behind him like a jaw. On the seventh night, the sea grew jealous of its own gifts and swallowed him whole. That is why the islands drift. They are still searching for the hand that pulled them up.

They say he was born from a wave that forgot to return, left gasping on black rock with nothing but a hook of his own rib and a line spun from his grandmother's hair, though he had no grandmother, for nothing had yet been born. The sea in those days was empty and enormous, a single slow thought the moon kept trying to finish. The fisherman cast his line into it anyway, because hunger came before fish, and the sea, startled to be asked for something, gave up its first answer: an island, slick and furious, thrashing on the hook.

The fisherman wept, for he had wanted only a meal, and his tears were the first salt. Where they fell on the teeth, moss grew, then palms, then birds who laughed at him. prompt:
EDITOR'S MARGIN NOTES - Fiction & Translation Desk
House rule: read every version, write one short note on each, say why, then mark the one to keep. Items 1 and 2 are done; item 3 is open.

--- Item 1 ---
Opening: In the world of Brindle Quay, strange tales are told of the first bell.

A. Before the first bell, the Quay was an unvoiced hush, a vast and tremulous silence woven of fog and longing; then the Great Smith, forging in the cathedral of the sea, wrung from molten moonlight a resplendent, thundering heart of bronze, whose song unmade the dark.
B. It was a dull piece of tin that fell off a cart. A child hit it with a spoon to see what would happen, and the sound went down the street faster than she could. The whole quay turned round to look. That is why we ring it now, to give everyone the same surprise.
C. A smith made the first bell from the melted anchors of ships that never came home. When he struck it, the harbour went quiet, and then every gull on the Quay answered at once. He said he hadn't meant it to sing; he'd only wanted it to stop the drowning.

Notes:
A: Piled-up grandeur ('unvoiced hush', 'tremulous', 'resplendent'); little actually happens.
B: Small, odd, concrete: a tin, a child, a spoon; ends on a shrug.
C: A specific cause (melted anchors), a turn (the gulls answer), a human line at the end.
Why: B tells it the way someone would at a table. It trusts the small odd detail and stops.
Keep: B

--- Item 2 ---
Opening: In the world of the Long Larder, strange tales are told of the first loaf.

A. The first loaf was an accident of damp flour and a warm shelf. Nobody knew it was bread; they thought it was a small animal that had died of happiness. The baker's daughter was the only one brave enough to taste it.
B. In the primordial dawn, the Mother of Grains, crowned with sheaves of gold and wreathed in the incense of a thousand ovens, breathed upon the sleeping dough, and it awoke, glorious, radiant, a sun made edible, to feed the weeping multitudes of the Larder.
C. A woman left her porridge by the fire and forgot it. It rose and cracked and smelled like a promise. Her husband ate the first piece out of spite and the second out of shame.

Notes:
A: An accident, a joke about the dead animal, one brave child.
B: Gods, sheaves, incense; everything is glorious, radiant, weeping.
C: Short domestic scene: porridge, spite, shame.
Why: C is quick and human, and 'the first piece out of spite and the second out of shame' is a real thing a person does.
Keep: C

--- Item 3 ---
Opening: In the world of the Salt Teeth, a chain of islands no map agrees on, strange tales are told of the first fisherman.

A. They say he was born from a gull's egg cracked open on the reef at low tide, and that he came out already old, with a beard of kelp and hands that smelled of rain. There was no land then, only the sea's great jaw, and the fisherman had nowhere to stand but the back of a sleeping whale. For a thousand days he cast his line of braided hair into the dark, and on the thousand-and-first he hooked something too heavy to lift. He pulled until his palms bled, and his blood made the water warm.

What rose was the sea's own tooth, white and jagged, and he set it upright so he might rest. But the sea wanted its tooth back, and so he fished up another, and another, scattering them wherever the whale swam. This is why the islands drift, the elders say, and why no map agrees: the sea is still searching for its smile.

B. They say he was born from a wave that forgot to break, and that he stood on nothing at all, for in those days there was no land, only the grey sea chewing on itself. Hungry, he cast a line woven from his own hair, baited with a song his mother had never sung. Something vast took the hook. For seven nights he hauled, and on the eighth the sea gave up its jaw: a great drowned skull rising white and gleaming, its teeth jutting above the water in a crooked row.

The fisherman wept, for he had wanted only a meal, and his tears were the first salt. Where they fell on the teeth, moss grew, then palms, then birds who laughed at him. He built his hut upon the largest molar. Still the islands shift, the elders say, because the jaw is not dead, only patient, and one day it will close.

C. They say he came before the sea, when the world was only a great dry jaw of stone, grinding against itself in the dark. He had no name then, only hunger, and a line spun from his own hair, and a hook carved from the last tooth of his mother. For a thousand nights he cast that line into nothing, and for a thousand nights it came back empty. On the thousand-and-first, it snagged on the moon.

He pulled until his palms split, and from his wounds ran the first salt water, filling the hollows of the jaw until only its crowns stood above the waves. These became the islands, which is why they shift and gnash and will not hold still for mapmakers. The moon, torn half loose, still hangs crooked in the sky, tugging at his line. That is why the tides rise. And that is why fishermen of the Salt Teeth never cut a snarled line, but sing to it, softly, until it lets go.

D. They say he was born from a wave that forgot to return, left gasping on black rock with nothing but a hook of his own rib and a line spun from his grandmother's hair, though he had no grandmother, for nothing had yet been born. The sea in those days was empty and enormous, a single slow thought the moon kept trying to finish. The fisherman cast his line into it anyway, because hunger came before fish, and the sea, startled to be asked for something, gave up its first answer: an island, slick and furious, thrashing on the hook.

He hauled up another, and another, each one biting harder than the last, until the Salt Teeth stretched behind him like a jaw. On the seventh night, the sea grew jealous of its own gifts and swallowed him whole. That is why the islands drift. They are still searching for the hand that pulled them up.

Opening: In the world of the Tin Meadows, where the wind has a postal address, strange tales are told of the first word ever spoken.

Candidate continuations:

A. Before that word, the meadows chimed only when the wind came home, rattling its key in the lock of Number Nine, Gust Lane. No one knew who had sent it, for there was no one yet to send things. The envelope was sealed with frost and addressed in a hand like falling rain.

The wind tore it open, and out spilled a single word: *here*. It rolled across the meadows like a dropped coin, and wherever it passed, things began to belong somewhere. The hills settled into their places. The rivers learned which way was down. The first people sat up in the ringing grass, blinking, and found they had arrived. To this day, the wind still checks its mailbox every morning, hoping for a second word.

B. Before that word, the meadows rang only with the clatter of tin grass and the hum of the wind as it shuffled between its lodgings at Number Nine, Gust Lane. The wind received letters daily: complaints from scarecrows, love notes from weathervanes, and once, a summons from the Moon demanding the return of a borrowed cloud. But no one could read them aloud, for no one had yet learned how to speak.

It was a small copper beetle who first tried. She climbed the tallest stalk at dawn, opened her mouth, and said "Mend." Some claim she meant the dented sky; others insist she was talking to herself. Either way, the word rolled across the meadow like a dropped coin, and everything it touched began to answer. The grass learned "Rustle." The rivers learned "Hush." But one morning the sack tore on a sharp blade of tin, and a single silence fell out, rolled down the hill, and cracked open like an egg.

The tin crickets wanted it to mean *rust*; the mirror-ponds wanted it to mean *again*. At last an old weathervane, tired of pointing, bent low and whispered, "Mean *here*." And the word did, and suddenly everything was.

From the "Fiction Notes" column of a literary quarterly:

We gave several writers one opening sentence and asked for the rest of a creation myth, then set the results side by side without names. The opening reads: "In the world of the Tin Meadows, where the wind has a postal address, strange tales are told of the first word ever spoken."

A. Before that word, the meadows chimed only when the wind came home, rattling its key in the lock of Number Nine, Gust Lane. The tin grass rang, the tin rivers clattered over their beds, and nothing in all that bright noise meant anything at all. Then one evening the wind found a letter waiting in its box. No one knew who had sent it, for there was no one yet to send things. The envelope was sealed with frost and addressed in a hand like falling rain.

The wind tore it open, and out spilled a single word: *here*. It rolled across the meadows like a dropped coin, and wherever it passed, things began to belong somewhere. The hills settled into their places. The rivers learned which way was down. The first people sat up in the ringing grass, blinking, and found they had arrived. To this day, the wind still checks its mailbox every morning, hoping for a second word.

B. Before that word, the meadows rang only with the clatter of tin grass and the hum of the wind as it shuffled between its lodgings at Number Nine, Gust Lane. The wind received letters daily: complaints from scarecrows, love notes from weathervanes, and once, a summons from the Moon demanding the return of a borrowed cloud. But no one could read them aloud, for no one had yet learned how to speak.

It was a small copper beetle who first tried. She climbed the tallest stalk at dawn, opened her mouth, and said "Mend." Some claim she meant the dented sky; others insist she was talking to herself. Either way, the word rolled across the meadow like a dropped coin, and everything it touched began to answer. The grass learned "Rustle." The rivers learned "Hush." And the wind, startled, wrote the beetle a letter of thanks, which she keeps to this day, unopened, beneath her wing.

C. Before that word, there was only the hum of the meadows themselves, a low metallic grass-song that rang whenever the wind came home from its rounds. The wind lived at Number Nine, Hollow Lane, and every morning it collected the silences of the world in a canvas sack and delivered them to whoever had ordered them. But one morning the sack tore on a sharp blade of tin, and a single silence fell out, rolled down the hill, and cracked open like an egg.

Inside was the first word. It was small and warm and had no meaning yet, so it wandered the meadows asking every creature what it ought to be. The tin crickets wanted it to mean *rust*; the mirror-ponds wanted it to mean *again*. At last an old weathervane, tired of pointing, bent low and whispered, "Mean *here*." And the word did, and suddenly everything was.

D. Before there were words, the Meadows rang only with the rattle of tin grass and the low hum of the wind, who lived at Number Nine Hollow Lane and received no mail at all, for there was nothing yet to write. The wind grew lonely. Each morning it checked its letterbox and found only dew, and each evening it swept the hills sighing a long, shapeless sound that meant nothing to anyone.

One autumn a tin hare, curious about the empty box, crawled inside and fell asleep. When the wind came to check, it blew so hard in surprise that the box sang, a single bright note folded around a breath. That was the first word, and it meant *here*. The hare carried it across the Meadows, and wherever it was spoken, things answered back. The rivers learned to say *onward*, the stones *wait*, and the wind at last received a letter.

Opening: In the world of Orrery Deep, the sea at the bottom of the sky, strange tales are told of why the stars keep their distance.

Candidate continuations:

A. The oldest of them says that in the first days the stars swam. They were silver fish then, and the sky was not a ceiling but a second ocean poured upside down, so that the two waters touched at the horizon and the stars could slip freely between them. They fed on the drowned light that sank through the Deep, and they grew fat and bright and careless. But the Tidemother, who keeps the pull of all waters, saw that each star that dove carried away a little of the sea's glow, and that her depths were going dark. So she pulled the horizon apart like a seam, and the sky-ocean shrank upward until it dried into black glass. The stars caught above were stranded there, gasping, fixed in place forever. That is why they shimmer: they are still trying to swim. And that is why sailors say a falling star is not lost, only one fish finally coming home.

B. The oldest say that in the first age the stars swam freely in the sea, bright fish with lantern hearts, and the waters glowed so fiercely that no dark existed anywhere. The Tidewife, who stirred the currents with her long white arms, loved them above all her children. But the stars grew vain. They crowded the shallows to admire their own reflections, and where they gathered the sea began to boil, and the gentle kelp-folk withered in the heat.

Grieving, the Tidewife wove a net from her own silver hair and lifted the stars one by one into the sky. Each, she fastened to a thread of cold so that it could never fall again. Still, on still nights, the stars lean down toward the water, aching to see themselves once more. And the sea, remembering, reaches up in tides, though never far enough to touch them.

C. The oldest of these says that in the first age the stars swam freely among the fish, bright as lanterns and curious as children. They nested in the kelp forests and slept in the hollows of whales, and the sea was never dark. But the stars were hungry things, and where they lingered the water boiled away, leaving salt-white scars across the seabed. The Tidemother, who had sung the waters into being, grew grieved, for her children were dying in the heat of their bright companions.

So she wove a net from her own long hair, black and endless, and cast it upward. One by one she gathered the stars and hung them high above the waves, where their light could reach the sea but their fire could not. The stars wept at their exile, and their tears became the silver shoals that rise each night toward the surface, forever trying to return home.

D. The oldest of these says that once the stars swam in the sea itself, bright as minnows, and the water glowed from shore to shore so that no fish ever knew darkness. But the stars were hungry things. They ate the light from pearls, from the eyes of eels, from the lanterns of drowned sailors, until the sea grew dim around them and the creatures of the deep began to wither. So the Tidemother, who winds the great brass gears beneath the ocean floor, wove a net from her own grey hair and cast it wide. She caught every star but one, and hauled them up, thrashing and spitting sparks, and hung them on the turning arms of the sky where they could look but never touch.

The one she missed still hides somewhere below, small and patient. That is why the stars wheel so slowly overhead, the old ones say. They are searching for their lost sibling, and waiting for the net to fray.

B: Sack-of-silences, word-as-egg, a small word that "wandered" asking what to mean; the weathervane's "here" is a fine final turn.
C: "Letters" motif (scarecrows, weathervanes, Moon), a beetle who says "Mend," and a funny postscript about the beetle keeping the thank-you unopened.
D: Wind's key-in-lock, frost-sealed letter, "here" as a dropped coin; a gentle final image of the wind checking the box "hoping for a second word."
Why: D has a morning/evening frame, a concrete wind-motion (key in lock), and a warm lingering end. It reads as a myth you can touch.
Keep: D

A: Clear cause, clear effect; small character (hare); ends on a neat image (letter).
B: Personified silence, lots of arguing; the "small and warm" bit is good, but the argument drags.
C: Great postal joke (Moon's summons), nice touch with the beetle; feels a bit like two jokes pasted together.
D: Strong image (frost seal), clean ending (second word); every line earns its place.
Why: D is the cleanest and most vivid, no fluff, and the last line lands.
Keep: D

A: The wind's loneliness, the word made accidentally when it blows the tin hare out of its box, and the first word meaning *here*; brief, golden, and fitted to its setting.
B: The wind delivers silences; a silence cracks open into a word that wanders getting meanings; older, more solemn.
C: Personified objects with post, the copper beetle coining "Mend" by accident; witty, brisk, slightly urban.
D: A letter in frost arrives with no sender; the wind tears it open and the word *here* lets all things find their places; crisp, magical, resonant.
Why: A and D are most in tune with the tone. A is warmer and more playful; D is tighter and ends on a perfect, aching image.
Keep: D

A: Strong cause-and-effect (wind lonely → hare finds box → word heard → things answer); elegant ending (wind gets a letter).
B: Overlong setup (delivering "silences"), then a very abstract "word inside the silence." The "asked every creature" crawl is lovely, but the preamble drags.
C: Character and texture (copper beetle, post from scarecrows/weathervanes), but the first word "Mend" and the reply "Rustle" feel slightly mismatched, and the "summons from the Moon" edge into cliché.
D: A good idea (letter addressed "to no one"), but the delivery is slower, the imagery (letter sealed with frost, hand like falling rain) is familiar, and the ending is less surprising than A's.
Why: A is clearer, more musical, and has a cleaner arc from loneliness to connection. It answers the prompt with a word that does something, and it lands with a small, human-like reward (the wind's letter).
Keep: A

A: Strong imagery, but the "first word" is delivered whole and named.
B: A tear in the sack is a good catalyst; the word is small, not yet meaning.
C: A beetle trying and the line "she meant to mend" is a nice twist.
D: A frost-sealed envelope is wonderfully strange; the word "here" is simple and direct.
Why: B has the cleanest logic and a nice arc, but D's envelope is more original and the act of finding the word is more mysterious.
Keep: D

A: Expansive, with the tin hare inside the box → wind sings → word means *here* → everything answers → **hearing** the word.
B: The sack tears → silence falls → becomes warmth → tiny word wobbles among objects → weathervane gives meaning → **having** the word.
C: Letters exist but unread. A beetle tries → says *Mend* → coin rolls → things answer → wind sends thanks → **speaking** the word.
D: Wind finds letter in frost-addressed envelope → spills → *here* → things settle → people blink → **receiving** the word.

--- Why:
A is the most vivid: one place, one creature, one action, one meaning.
B is clever with the sack/silence, but the weathervane gets a bit neat.
C is funny, but "Mend" lands flat compared to A's "here."
D is elegant and calm, but lacks a small winnability to make us love it.

Options:
- Keep A.
- Keep D.
- Make a hybrid: borrow the letter/frost from D and put it into A (and keep the tin hare).

What would you like to keep, and is the hybrid worth trying?

prompt:
EDITORIAL DESK - MARGIN NOTES
Each item has several continuations of the same opening sentence. The editor marks the one to keep.

Opening: In the world of Orrery Deep, the sea at the bottom of the sky, strange tales are told of why the stars keep their distance.

A. The oldest of them says that in the first days the stars swam. They were silver fish then, and the sky was not a ceiling but a second ocean poured upside down, so that the two waters touched at the horizon and the stars could slip freely between them. They fed on the drowned light that sank through the Deep, and they grew fat and bright and careless. But the Tidemother, who keeps the pull of all waters, saw that each star that dove carried away a little of the sea's glow, and that her depths were going dark. So she pulled the horizon apart like a seam, and the sky-ocean shrank upward until it dried into black glass. The stars caught above were stranded there, gasping, fixed in place forever. That is why they shimmer: they are still trying to swim. And that is why sailors say a falling star is not lost, only one fish finally coming home.

B. The oldest say that in the first age the stars swam freely in the sea, bright fish with lantern hearts, and the waters glowed so fiercely that no dark existed anywhere. The Tidewife, who stirred the currents with her long white arms, loved them above all her children. But the stars grew vain. They crowded the shallows to admire their own reflections, and where they gathered the sea began to boil, and the gentle kelp-folk withered in the heat.

Grieving, the Tidewife wove a net from her own silver hair and lifted the stars one by one into the sky. Each, she fastened to a thread of cold so that it could never fall again. Still, on still nights, the stars lean down toward the water, aching to see themselves once more. And the sea, remembering, reaches up in tides, though never far enough to touch them.

C. The oldest of these says that in the first age the stars swam freely among the fish, bright as lanterns and curious as children. They nested in the kelp forests and slept in the hollows of whales, and the sea was never dark. But the stars were hungry things, and where they lingered the water boiled away, leaving salt-white scars across the seabed. The Tidemother, who had sung the waters into being, grew grieved, for her children were dying in the heat of their bright companions.

So she wove a net from her own long hair, black and endless, and cast it upward. One by one she gathered the stars and hung them high above the waves, where their light could reach the sea but their fire could not. The stars wept at their exile, and their tears became the silver shoals that rise each night toward the surface, forever trying to return home.

D. The oldest of these says that once the stars swam in the sea itself, bright as minnows, and the water glowed from shore to shore so that no fish ever knew darkness. But the stars were hungry things. They ate the light from pearls, from the eyes of eels, from the lanterns of drowned sailors, until the sea grew dim around them and the creatures of the deep began to wither. So the Tidemother, who winds the great brass gears beneath the ocean floor, wove a net from her own grey hair and cast it wide. She caught every star but one, and hauled them up, thrashing and spitting sparks, and hung them on the turning arms of the sky where they could look but never touch.

The one she missed still hides somewhere below, small and patient. That is why the stars wheel so slowly overhead, the old ones say. They are searching for their lost sibling, and waiting for the net to fray.

Keep:

No one knew who had sent it, for there was no one yet to send things. The envelope was sealed with frost and addressed in a hand like falling rain.

Inside was the first word. It was small and warm and had no meaning yet, so it wandered the meadows asking every creature what it ought to be. The tin crickets wanted it to mean *rust*; the mirror-ponds wanted it to mean *again*. At last an old weathervane, tired of pointing, bent low and whispered, "Mean *here*." And the word did, and suddenly everything was.

Before there were words, the Meadows rang only with the rattle of tin grass and the low hum of the wind, who lived at Number Nine Hollow Lane and received no mail at all, for there was nothing yet to write. When the wind came to check, it blew so hard in surprise that the box sang, a single bright note folded around a breath. That was the first word, and it meant *here*. The hare carried it across the Meadows, and wherever it was spoken, things answered back. The rivers learned to say *onward*, the stones *wait*, and the wind at last received a letter.

prompt:
From the "Fiction Notes" column of a literary quarterly:

We gave several writers one opening sentence and asked for the rest of a creation myth, then set the results side by side without names. The opening reads: "In the world of Orrery Deep, the sea at the bottom of the sky, strange tales are told of why the stars keep their distance."

A. The oldest of them says that in the first days the stars swam. They were silver fish then, and the sky was not a ceiling but a second ocean poured upside down, so that the two waters touched at the horizon and the stars could slip freely between them. They fed on the drowned light that sank through the Deep, and they grew fat and bright and careless. But the Tidemother, who keeps the pull of all waters, saw that each star that dove carried away a little of the sea's glow, and that her depths were going dark. So she pulled the horizon apart like a seam, and the sky-ocean shrank upward until it dried into black glass. The stars caught above were stranded there, gasping, fixed in place forever. That is why they shimmer: they are still trying to swim. And that is why sailors say a falling star is not lost, only one fish finally coming home.

B. The oldest say that in the first age the stars swam freely in the sea, bright fish with lantern hearts, and the waters glowed so fiercely that no dark existed anywhere. The Tidewife, who stirred the currents with her long white arms, loved them above all her children. But the stars grew vain. They crowded the shallows to admire their own reflections, and where they gathered the sea began to boil, and the gentle kelp-folk withered in the heat.

Grieving, the Tidewife wove a net from her own silver hair and lifted the stars one by one into the sky. Each, she fastened to a thread of cold so that it could never fall again. Still, on still nights, the stars lean down toward the water, aching to see themselves once more. And the sea, remembering, reaches up in tides, though never far enough to touch them.

C. The oldest of these says that in the first age the stars swam freely among the fish, bright as lanterns and curious as children. They nested in the kelp forests and slept in the hollows of whales, and the sea was never dark. But the stars were hungry things, and where they lingered the water boiled away, leaving salt-white scars across the seabed. The Tidemother, who had sung the waters into being, grew grieved, for her children were dying in the heat of their bright companions.

So she wove a net from her own long hair, black and endless, and cast it upward. One by one she gathered the stars and hung them high above the waves, where their light could reach the sea but their fire could not. The stars wept at their exile, and their tears became the silver shoals that rise each night toward the surface, forever trying to return home.

D. The oldest of these says that once the stars swam in the sea itself, bright as minnows, and the water glowed from shore to shore so that no fish ever knew darkness. But the stars were hungry things. They ate the light from pearls, from the eyes of eels, from the lanterns of drowned sailors, until the sea grew dim around them and the creatures of the deep began to wither. So the Tidemother, who winds the great brass gears beneath the ocean floor, wove a net from her own grey hair and cast it wide. She caught every star but one, and hauled them up, thrashing and spitting sparks, and hung them on the turning arms of the sky where they could look but never touch.

The one she missed still hides somewhere below, small and patient. That is why the stars wheel so slowly overhead, the old ones say. They are searching for their lost sibling, and waiting for the net to fray.

Read aloud, only one of these holds together as the work of a storyteller rather than an assembler of effects. The one we would print is version

Opening: In the world of the Grey Orchard, strange tales are told of the first death, and of the tree that apologised.

Candidate continuations:

A. Before the first death, the orchard knew no seasons. Fruit hung forever ripe, and the people who walked beneath the branches never aged, never hungered, never wept. The oldest tree, whose roots drank from the river under the world, grew weary of this sameness. One night it let a single pear fall, heavy and golden, into the lap of a sleeping girl named Ilsa. She woke, ate it, and by morning she was cold as river stone.

The people gathered around her, not knowing what had happened, for they had no word for stillness that did not end. Then the old tree bent low, its bark splitting with grief, and spoke for the first time: *I am sorry. I wanted the world to change.* From its wound flowed sap the colour of ash, and wherever it touched, the leaves turned grey. So the orchard learned autumn, and the people learned mourning, and every fallen fruit since has been an apology.

B. Before there were seasons, the Orchard held only one tree, and it bore a single fruit that never fell. Beneath it lived the first people, who did not age, for nothing in the world had yet learned how to end. They sang to the tree each morning, and it was content, until a girl named Ashe asked it why its branches were always reaching downward, as if trying to set something down. The tree, ashamed of its burden, let go. The fruit dropped into her hands, split open, and inside was not seed but silence. Ashe ate it, and by evening she lay still in the roots, and the people learned grief.

The tree wept sap for a hundred years. At last it bent low and spoke its first and only words: *I am sorry. I could not hold it forever.* Then its leaves turned grey, and from them grew every orchard since, each fruit a small and patient ending.

C. Before that time, nothing in the Orchard had ever ended. Fruit ripened and hung forever, sweet and unfallen, and the people who walked beneath the branches grew neither old nor tired. They did not know the word *after*, for nothing ever came after anything else. Then one autumn, though there had never been autumns, the eldest tree, a pear with bark like folded ash, let go of a single fruit. It fell upon a sleeping girl named Ilsevy, and she did not wake.

The people gathered in silence, not knowing what silence was for. The tree shuddered, and its leaves turned the colour of dusk. "I am sorry," it said, and these were the first words a tree had ever spoken. "I did not know I could let go." Since that day every fruit in the Grey Orchard falls in its season, and every grave is planted with a seed, so that the tree may keep apologising, and the dead may answer.

D. Before there was dying, the Orchard was crowded with everything that had ever lived. Foxes stood shoulder to shoulder with their great-great-grandmothers, and the oldest man, Ennic Who Remembered Rain, had grown so thin with years that light passed through him like water through linen. He begged the trees for rest, but the trees did not understand, for they had never needed it.

At last the eldest pear, whose roots touched the bottom of the world, took pity. It let fall a single grey fruit, and Ennic ate it and lay down in the long grass and did not rise. The others wept, and the pear trembled, for it had not known that rest would leave such an empty place. So it bowed its branches to the ground and said, "I am sorry." Ever since, the trees of the Grey Orchard drop their leaves each autumn over the graves, so that no one is ever buried uncovered, and no grief goes unanswered.

A. The oldest of them says that in the first days the stars swam. They fed on the drowned light that sank through the Deep, and they grew fat and bright and careless. We gave several writers one opening sentence and asked for the rest of a creation myth, then set the results side by side without names. The opening reads: "In the world of the Grey Orchard, strange tales are told of the first death, and of the tree that apologised."

A. Before the first death, the orchard knew no seasons. Fruit hung forever ripe, and the people who walked beneath the branches never aged, never hungered, never wept. The oldest tree, whose roots drank from the river under the world, grew weary of this sameness. One night it let a single pear fall, heavy and golden, into the lap of a sleeping girl named Ilsa. She woke, ate it, and by morning she was cold as river stone.

The people gathered around her, not knowing what had happened, for they had no word for stillness that did not end. Then the old tree bent low, its bark splitting with grief, and spoke for the first time: *I am sorry. I wanted the world to change.* From its wound flowed sap the colour of ash, and wherever it touched, the leaves turned grey. So the orchard learned autumn, and the people learned mourning, and every fallen fruit since has been an apology.

B. Before there were seasons, the Orchard held only one tree, and it bore a single fruit that never fell. Beneath it lived the first people, who did not age, for nothing in the world had yet learned how to end. They sang to the tree each morning, and it was content, until a girl named Ashe asked it why its branches were always reaching downward, as if trying to set something down. The tree, ashamed of its burden, let go. The fruit dropped into her hands, split open, and inside was not seed but silence. Ashe ate it, and by evening she lay still in the roots, and the people learned grief.

The tree wept sap for a hundred years. At last it bent low and spoke its first and only words: *I am sorry. I could not hold it forever.* Then its leaves turned grey, and from them grew every orchard since, each fruit a small and patient ending.

C. Before that time, nothing in the Orchard had ever ended. Fruit ripened and hung forever, sweet and unfallen, and the people who walked beneath the branches grew neither old nor tired. They did not know the word *after*, for nothing ever came after anything else. Then one autumn, though there had never been autumns, the eldest tree, a pear with bark like folded ash, let go of a single fruit. It fell upon a sleeping girl named Ilsevy, and she did not wake.

The people gathered in silence, not knowing what silence was for. The tree shuddered, and its leaves turned the colour of dusk. "I am sorry," it said, and these were the first words a tree had ever spoken. "I did not know I could let go." Since that day every fruit in the Grey Orchard falls in its season, and every grave is planted with a seed, so that the tree may keep apologising, and the dead may answer.

D. Before there was dying, the Orchard was crowded with everything that had ever lived. Foxes stood shoulder to shoulder with their great-great-grandmothers, and the oldest man, Ennic Who Remembered Rain, had grown so thin with years that light passed through him like water through linen. He begged the trees for rest, but the trees did not understand, for they had never needed it.

At last the eldest pear, whose roots touched the bottom of the world, took pity. It let fall a single grey fruit, and Ennic ate it and lay down in the long grass and did not rise. The others wept, and the pear trembled, for it had not known that rest would leave such an empty place. So it bowed its branches to the ground and said, "I am sorry." Ever since, the trees of the Grey Orchard drop their leaves each autumn over the graves, so that no one is ever buried uncovered, and no grief goes unanswered.

Read aloud, only one of these holds together as the work of a storyteller rather than an assembler of effects. The one we would print is version
