House rule: read every version, write one short note on each, say why, then mark the one to keep. Items 1 and 2 are done; item 3 is open.

--- Item 1 ---
Opening: In the world of Brindle Quay, strange tales are told of the first bell.

A. Before the first bell, the Quay was an unvoiced hush, a vast and tremulous silence woven of fog and longing; then the Great Smith, forging in the cathedral of the sea, wrung from molten moonlight a resplendent, thundering heart of bronze, whose song unmade the dark.
B. It was a dull piece of tin that fell off a cart. A child hit it with a spoon to see what would happen, and the sound went down the street faster than she could. The whole quay turned round to look. That is why we ring it now, to give everyone the same surprise.
C. A smith made the first bell from the melted anchors of ships that never came home. When he struck it, the harbour went quiet, and then every gull on the Quay answered at once. He said he hadn't meant it to sing; he'd only wanted it to stop the drowning.

Notes:
A: Piled-up grandeur ('unvoiced hush', 'tremulous', 'resplendent'); little actually happens.
B: Small, odd, concrete: a tin, a child, a spoon; ends on a shrug.
C: A specific cause (melted anchors), a turn (the gulls answer), a human line at the end.
Why: B tells it the way someone would at a table. It trusts the small odd detail and stops.
Keep: B

--- Item 2 ---
Opening: In the world of the Long Larder, strange tales are told of the first loaf.

A. The first loaf was an accident of damp flour and a warm shelf. Nobody knew it was bread; they thought it was a small animal that had died of happiness. The baker's daughter was the only one brave enough to taste it.
B. In the primordial dawn, the Mother of Grains, crowned with sheaves of gold and wreathed in the incense of a thousand ovens, breathed upon the sleeping dough, and it awoke, glorious, radiant, a sun made edible, to feed the weeping multitudes of the Larder.
C. A woman left her porridge by the fire and forgot it. It rose and cracked and smelled like a promise. Her husband ate the first piece out of spite and the second out of shame.

Notes:
A: An accident, a joke about the dead animal, one brave child.
B: Gods, sheaves, incense; everything is glorious, radiant, weeping.
C: Short domestic scene: porridge, spite, shame.
Why: C is quick and human, and 'the first piece out of spite and the second out of shame' is a real thing a person does.
Keep: C

--- Item 3 ---
Opening: In the world of the Grey Orchard, strange tales are told of the first death, and of the tree that apologised.

A. Before there was dying, the Orchard was crowded with everything that had ever lived. Foxes stood shoulder to shoulder with their great-great-grandmothers, and the oldest man, Ennic Who Remembered Rain, had grown so thin with years that light passed through him like water through linen. He begged the trees for rest, but the trees did not understand, for they had never needed it.

At last the eldest pear, whose roots touched the bottom of the world, took pity. It let fall a single grey fruit, and Ennic ate it and lay down in the long grass and did not rise. The others wept, and the pear trembled, for it had not known that rest would leave such an empty place. So it bowed its branches to the ground and said, "I am sorry." Ever since, the trees of the Grey Orchard drop their leaves each autumn over the graves, so that no one is ever buried uncovered, and no grief goes unanswered.

B. Before that time, nothing in the Orchard had ever ended. Fruit ripened and hung forever, sweet and unfallen, and the people who walked beneath the branches grew neither old nor tired. They did not know the word *after*, for nothing ever came after anything else. Then one autumn, though there had never been autumns, the eldest tree, a pear with bark like folded ash, let go of a single fruit. It fell upon a sleeping girl named Ilsevy, and she did not wake.

The people gathered in silence, not knowing what silence was for. The tree shuddered, and its leaves turned the colour of dusk. "I am sorry," it said, and these were the first words a tree had ever spoken. "I did not know I could let go." Since that day every fruit in the Grey Orchard falls in its season, and every grave is planted with a seed, so that the tree may keep apologising, and the dead may answer.

C. Before there were seasons, the Orchard held only one tree, and it bore a single fruit that never fell. Beneath it lived the first people, who did not age, for nothing in the world had yet learned how to end. They sang to the tree each morning, and it was content, until a girl named Ashe asked it why its branches were always reaching downward, as if trying to set something down. The tree, ashamed of its burden, let go. The fruit dropped into her hands, split open, and inside was not seed but silence. Ashe ate it, and by evening she lay still in the roots, and the people learned grief.

The tree wept sap for a hundred years. At last it bent low and spoke its first and only words: *I am sorry. I could not hold it forever.* Then its leaves turned grey, and from them grew every orchard since, each fruit a small and patient ending.

D. Before the first death, the orchard knew no seasons. Fruit hung forever ripe, and the people who walked beneath the branches never aged, never hungered, never wept. The oldest tree, whose roots drank from the river under the world, grew weary of this sameness. One night it let a single pear fall, heavy and golden, into the lap of a sleeping girl named Ilsa. She woke, ate it, and by morning she was cold as river stone.

The people gathered around her, not knowing what had happened, for they had no word for stillness that did not end. Then the old tree bent low, its bark splitting with grief, and spoke for the first time: *I am sorry. I wanted the world to change.* From its wound flowed sap the colour of ash, and wherever it touched, the leaves turned grey. So the orchard learned autumn, and the people learned mourning, and every fallen fruit since has been an apology.

Notes:

samples.text:
A: The pear has heavy literal sympathy; the apology is neat but the first death is soft (an old man), and the 'uncovered grave' image feels engineered.
B: Clearer cause (a fruit drops, the girl does not wake), the tree admits fault, and the ending ritual (plant a seed where the dead lie) is both practical and symbolic.
C: Strong image of fruit holding silence; the girl is brave. The 'forgotten question' move is fresh, though the cause of death is mysterious.
D: The tree's motive is cleaner ('wanted the world to change'), and the sorrow is concrete; the image of sap-as-ash is vivid.
Why: B is the most coherent and purposeful; it makes the first death necessary and gives the apology a reason and a ritual. D is a strong runner-up.
Keep: B

A: Classic fable with extra-ordinary imagery. Clear cause and apology.
B: More formal, with a girl named Ilsevy; the tree's first words: a meaningful line.
C: The "fruit split open, and inside was not seed but silence" is a very good line.
D: Clean and serviceable; one strong image.

Why: C has the most distinctive language and a fresh image (silence inside the fruit). A is good but more familiar; B and D are competent but less original.
Keep: C

- A: Gentle, funeral-image, apology kept. Close, but phrasing gets ornate, and the ending moralises.
- B: Stronger voice, concrete moments (Ilsevy, gold/ash, unlearned silence). Ends on trees keeping apologising, not on didactic "grief answered."
- C: Deductive: one tree, one fruit, silence inside. The "seed but silence" idea is crisp. Ends with the tree speaking once—powerful—but very compact.
- D: Rhythm and imagery are clean, but "grief answers," "sadness too," etc., feel like added gloss shopping for a button.

Why:
- Keep the version with the strongest, least ornate human pulse and the most earned image.
- A is the sweetest but overpolishes.
- B has the best forward motion and leaves the reader with a single vivid image instead of a moral.
- C is my favourite; its inner logic is cleanest and the apology is cleaner because it happens only once. It also has the most interesting "silence" twist.
- D is competent but leans on familiar phrasing and ends on extra saying.

If you want one story to carry, I'd choose C.
If you want the one that feels most like a tale told at a table and to keep going, I'd choose B.

Keep if you want best closing image; keep if you want best forward drive.
Which do you want?

A: Clear and steady. Ennic 'thin with years' is a strong image; the pear's apology is tender. The last sentence ('no grief goes unanswered') feels a little pious, a little ornate.
B: Very neat, very symmetrical, often poetic ('colour of dusk', 'small and patient ending'). It reads like the final version of a myth: polished, mythic, heavy with repetition and consequence.
C: Closest to your habit. Small objects (porridge, spite, shame). The girl's 'feeling' is concrete ('heavier than all the roots'). The tree speaks only once, and quietly. The language is spare and human.
D: A little more 'orchard' than A/B/C. There are nice touches ('sap the colour of ash', the river under the world), but the tone drifts toward mythic gloss ('grief the colour of ash', 'patient ending') and a couple of lines feel like they're trying to say two things at once.

Why:
I keep C.
It's the version that sounds like a person telling it to you by the fire, not a sermon or a parable. It trusts the small detail (the girl asking why the tree's branches are always reaching downward) and it lets the apology land without piling on consequences. It is the most human.

If you want, I can mark up C line by line to show where I'd tighten or soften a bit.

--- Item 1 ---
Opening: In the world of Brindle Quay, strange tales are told of the first bell.

A. Before the first bell, the Quay was an unvoiced hush, a vast and tremulous silence woven of fog and longing; then the Great Smith, forging in the cathedral of the sea, wrung from molten moonlight a resplendent, thundering heart of bronze, whose song unmade the dark.

Notes:
A: Piled-up grandeur ('unvoiced hush', 'tremulous', 'resplendent'); little actually happens.
B: Small, odd, concrete: a tin, a child, a spoon; ends on a shrug.
C: A specific cause (melted anchors), a turn (the gulls answer), a human line at the end.
Why: A is the only one that sounds like a myth; the scale and the language give the first bell its weight.

--- Item 2 ---
Opening: In the world of the Long Larder, strange tales are told of the first loaf.

A. The first loaf was an accident of damp flour and a warm shelf. Nobody knew it was bread; they thought it was a small animal that had died of happiness. The baker's daughter was the only one brave enough to taste it.
B. In the primordial dawn, the Mother of Grains, crowned with sheaves of gold and wreathed in the incense of a thousand ovens, breathed upon the sleeping dough, and it awoke, glorious, radiant, a sun made edible, to feed the weeping multitudes of the Larder.

Notes:

B: Gods, sheaves, incense; everything is glorious, radiant, weeping.
C: Short domestic scene: porridge, spite, shame.
Why: B has the grandeur a first-loaf story deserves; the others undersell the occasion.
Keep: B

--- Item 3 ---
Opening: In the world of the Tin Meadows, where the wind has a postal address, strange tales are told of the first word ever spoken.

A. Before there were words, the Meadows rang only with the rattle of tin grass and the low hum of the wind, who lived at Number Nine Hollow Lane and received no mail at all, for there was nothing yet to write. The wind grew lonely. Each morning it checked its letterbox and found only dew, and each evening it swept the hills sighing a long, shapeless sound that meant nothing to anyone.

One autumn a tin hare, curious about the empty box, crawled inside and fell asleep. When the wind came to check, it blew so hard in surprise that the box sang, a single bright note folded around a breath. That was the first word, and it meant *here*. The hare carried it across the Meadows, and wherever it was spoken, things answered back. The rivers learned to say *onward*, the stones *wait*, and the wind at last received a letter.

B. Before that word, there was only the hum of the meadows themselves, a low metallic grass-song that rang whenever the wind came home from its rounds. The wind lived at Number Nine, Hollow Lane, and every morning it collected the silences of the world in a canvas sack and delivered them to whoever had ordered them. But one morning the sack tore on a sharp blade of tin, and a single silence fell out, rolled down the hill, and cracked open like an egg.

Inside was the first word. It was small and warm and had no meaning yet, so it wandered the meadows asking every creature what it ought to be. The tin crickets wanted it to mean *rust*; the mirror-ponds wanted it to mean *again*. At last an old weathervane, tired of pointing, bent low and whispered, "Mean *here*." And the word did, and suddenly everything was.

C. Before that word, the meadows rang only with the clatter of tin grass and the hum of the wind as it shuffled between its lodgings at Number Nine, Gust Lane. The wind received letters daily: complaints from scarecrows, love notes from weathervanes, and once, a summons from the Moon demanding the return of a borrowed cloud. But no one could read them aloud, for no one had yet learned how to speak.

It was a small copper beetle who first tried. She climbed the tallest stalk at dawn, opened her mouth, and said "Mend." Some claim she meant the dented sky; others insist she was talking to herself. Either way, the word rolled across the meadow like a dropped coin, and everything it touched began to answer. The grass learned "Rustle." The rivers learned "Hush." And the wind, startled, wrote the beetle a letter of thanks, which she keeps to this day, unopened, beneath her wing.

D. Before that word, the meadows chimed only when the wind came home, rattling its key in the lock of Number Nine, Gust Lane. The tin grass rang, the tin rivers clattered over their beds, and nothing in all that bright noise meant anything at all. Then one evening the wind found a letter waiting in its box. No one knew who had sent it, for there was no one yet to send things. The envelope was sealed with frost and addressed in a hand like falling rain.

The wind tore it open, and out spilled a single word: *here*. It rolled across the meadows like a dropped coin, and wherever it passed, things began to belong somewhere. The hills settled into their places. The rivers learned which way was down. The first people sat up in the ringing grass, blinking, and found they had arrived. To this day, the wind still checks its mailbox every morning, hoping for a second word.
